ideas.risks: It is likely only sufficient, not necessary, because predictable long-tail rewards can be exploitable. It may also hide learnability assumptions inside process-specific quantities unavailable to a universal learner.
ideas.summary: Formalize the solver's value-tail modulus theorem: define B_T(H)=sup_a V_T(a)-sup_a V_T^H(a), replace max by sup, and prove the bound inf_{H,K}{sqrt(T(H+1)log K)+T/K+B_T(H)} with exact quantifiers. Then compare B_T(H) to the stronger raw tail quantity D_T(H)=sup_a E sum_t a 1{H<tau_t(a)<infty}. Look for examples separating beta, D_T, and B_T.
ideas.title: Value-Tail Modulus
ideas.why_promising: This turns the false beta-necessity conjecture into a precise positive theorem and gives a clean object that may be close to the right characterization.

ideas.risks: The decomposition may become tautological unless the predictable component is tied to an explicit algorithm or complexity measure. It may also depend heavily on whether the learner knows the process law.
ideas.summary: Decompose long-delayed reward into predictable and unpredictable parts relative to the learner's filtration after observing P_t. Study Y_t^H(a)=a 1{H<tau_t(a)<infty} and whether E[Y_t^H(a)|history] or a learnable surrogate can be competed with online. Aim for a condition like: truncatable value plus learnable predictable tail value is sufficient, while unpredictable tail value yields lower bounds.
ideas.title: Predictable Tail Decomposition
ideas.why_promising: The solver's obstruction says raw long tails are not fatal when the useful information is predictable; this direction targets exactly the missing term in a true iff statement.

ideas.risks: Lower bounds from two environments may prove only non-uniform or horizon-dependent impossibility. Care is needed to match the exact observation model and strict inequality P>a.
ideas.summary: Develop an indistinguishable-prefix lower-bound lemma. Construct pairs or packings of price processes whose histories are identical, or have small total variation, until late times but whose best fixed quotes differ by a constant and have linear value. Quantify regret in terms of value separation minus distinguishability of observed prefixes.
ideas.title: Indistinguishable Prefix Lower Bounds
ideas.why_promising: This gives a precise way to formalize when long-delayed value is not inferable, which is the main missing necessity mechanism in the solver attempt.

ideas.risks: The market-making reward class is monotone and one-dimensional, so generic delayed-expert lower bounds may not embed. The truncation term may be an upper-bound artifact in some stochastic models.
ideas.summary: Try to match the upper rate for polynomial or exponential tail profiles. For beta(h) about h^{-alpha}, construct renewal or block processes where the best quote has linear value but useful rewards arrive after heavy-tailed delays. Prove lower bounds of order comparable to inf_H sqrt(T H)+T beta(H), at least for two or finitely many separated quotes.
ideas.title: Tail-Rate Lower Bounds
ideas.why_promising: The current draft has rate upper bounds but no matching lower bounds. Even partial lower bounds would clarify whether the truncation tradeoff is fundamental.

ideas.risks: This is partly definitional, so it will not by itself solve the theorem. The payoff is only high if it produces concrete theorem variants and impossibility examples.
ideas.summary: Build a theorem matrix over quantifier choices: process fixed versus horizon-dependent, learner knowing T versus anytime, stochastic exogenous versus adaptive nonanticipating, process-known versus universal, and process-specific versus uniform-over-class regret. For each cell, record whether beta, B_T, or a prefix-indistinguishability condition is plausible, false, or sufficient.
ideas.title: Quantifier Taxonomy
ideas.why_promising: Many apparent contradictions are really model-choice issues. A precise taxonomy can prevent proving an iff theorem in the wrong model.

ideas.risks: This likely requires stronger stochastic assumptions such as stationarity, mixing, or parametric hazards. Without them, censored-feedback estimation may be impossible.
ideas.summary: Investigate algorithms that use censored long-delay information instead of truncating it: survival/hazard estimation for trade times, Kaplan-Meier-style estimates for quote values, or UCB over censored rewards. Target stochastic stationary or mixing price processes where uniform beta may fail but the reward curve is learnable from partial observations.
ideas.title: Censored-Feedback Algorithms
ideas.why_promising: If successful, this would show a genuine class of learnable problems beyond truncation and explain how predictable long tails can be exploited algorithmically.

ideas.risks: Discontinuities from the strict threshold reward may force grid-type approximations anyway. Improvements may be logarithmic or require atomlessness assumptions.
ideas.summary: Exploit the special reward geometry r_t(a)=a 1{a<M_t}. The comparator value is a times a tail distribution of future maxima. Explore adaptive discretization, quantile grids, VC/threshold-class analysis, or isotonic structure to replace the crude T/K discretization and log K expert bound.
ideas.title: Threshold Geometry
ideas.why_promising: The current upper bound treats quotes as generic experts after gridding, but the one-dimensional threshold structure may yield sharper rates or cleaner continuum proofs.

ideas.risks: Some examples may rely on learners knowing the process law, so they must be labeled carefully. Others may only refute overly strong candidate conditions.
ideas.summary: Create a catalogue of small counterexamples: beta fails but V_T^*=o(T); beta fails and B_T(H) is large but the sequence is deterministic/predictable; B_T(H) is small while D_T(H) is large; two processes share the same beta or B_T profile but have different learnability. Each example should state the quantifier model it refutes.
ideas.title: Counterexample Catalogue
ideas.why_promising: A true characterization will be shaped by separating examples. This is a low-coupling task that can quickly eliminate wrong iff candidates.

ideas.risks: The resulting condition may be abstract, involving sequential complexity rather than a simple tail profile. It may be too general for the intended paper theorem.
ideas.summary: Formulate the problem as online learning with delayed/censored full information over the function class f_m(a)=a 1{a<m}. Seek a minimax expression using sequential Rademacher complexity of the observable truncated game plus a tail/information modulus for unobserved rewards. Compare this to standard delayed expert bounds and partial-monitoring lower bounds.
ideas.title: Minimax Complexity Formulation
ideas.why_promising: If a simple tail iff is impossible, a minimax complexity statement may be the honest general characterization and can specialize to clean sufficient conditions.
